utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the court. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are going to proceed with the hearing. Let me greet the Prosecution, as well as the witness, the Defence counsel, the accused, and all people who assist us. I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Scott to proceed with the examination-in-chief; but before I do so, Mr. Scott, I have a very brief question to ask. I spent part of the night pouring over the documents you disclosed and the documents we discussed yesterday, and I identified the following problem: Looking at document 301, Rules of Military Discipline, this is document that was produced by Mr. Boban. It is a document that your investigator, Mr. Simon Leach found, and he stated that he had made a photocopy of the original copy of a document that is to be found in Zenica. The photocopy in B/C/S of these documents relates to a number of articles. But if we look at the English translation, Articles 5 and 6 have not been translated. It's something that should not have escaped you. You should have seen that Articles 6 and 7 had not been translated. If you look at the version in B/C/S, we have part of the document that has been whited out. So what happened? Is it your investigator who did a proof photocopy of the document, or was the original document that way? However, we seem to have to deal with an official document; therefore, you should have been in a position to find the original of this document in order to allow us to have a full translation of this, because I'm not in a position now to say what Articles 6 and 7 are all about. Here I just see "illegible." I'm not asking you to answer this question just now, but I wanted to draw your attention on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First of all, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and to all those in the courtroom, in and about the courtroom, including our translation staff. Your Honour, I can make further inquiry into it. I certainly can't say off the top of my head. Well, what I can say, based on some years of experience in dealing with these matters, is that it's very likely that was the best copy available, and that's, you know, in investigation, you take the documents, you take the evidence as you find it. Sometimes you can improve on it; sometimes you cannot. Having said that, I'll be happy, of course, to make further inquiry on whether an additional version of this document can be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, General Pringle.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I trust you had a reasonably pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you still have the documents in front of you, and if you could go back to where we left off yesterday, at least in terms of the same document, I want to move to a different topic, and if I can direct you to P 04020. Again, I'm moving past paragraph number 1; although, I suspect there will be further opportunity to discuss that. But if you look at paragraphs 2, 3, and 4, and just in this particular respect, in each of those paragraphs, and I believe the fourth line of the second paragraph, the second line of the third paragraph, and what would be the third line of paragraph 4 or the first - at least in the English version - the first line on the top of the second page, the word "Balija" is used. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me -- hoping to avoid perhaps some of the issues that were raised yesterday, assuming, assuming that "Balija" is a very derogatory term towards Muslims, and assuming that as of August of 1993, the HVO is in armed conflict with the ABiH and the Muslims, can you tell us what effect on the command climate it would have for a senior officer to issue an order using the terminology repeatedly, "Balija"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, it would give the impression that the senior officer issuing the order was certainly being derogatory about, in this case, I assume, Muslim forces. It would be the equivalent if one reflects back to the Vietnam War of perhaps an order being given about dealing with the Gooks or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what is the effect on troops when senior officers use that sort of terminology, in terms of what sort of message does it set or what effect does it have on discipline?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clearly sending a message that the -- that the senior commander regards the foe in a rather derogatory and dismissive way, and that can also send a subliminal message that therefore they can be treated in a way perhaps that is commensurate with their lowly status.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- Your Honour, if I could -- Your Honour, unless the gentleman can read minds, I suspect we should have some foundation on this. Clearly, you know, what he's talking about, the "subliminal message," unless he can tie this down factually, I think this should be stricken from the record. I find it offensive that we would have an officer of the British Army, retired be it, to be making these sorts of speculative and unfounded comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, Mr. Scott tried to exemplify your theory or your explanations about climate command. He used the example of this document where we see the word "Balija." In your statement, you stated that, by using derogatory terms, there can be an impact on those who have to obey the orders. You referred to the Vietnam War, and you stated that the -- when the American forces or the American forces used the word "Gooks" to identify the north Vietnamese, that could have an impact. In military colleges or academies, as part of the doctrine, as part of NATO or military studies, has any thought been given to the use of words, of certain vocabulary in orders? Is it your personal opinion, or are you talking on the basis of work, research that's been conducted before on the use of certain terms in -- in orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm drawing on my own experience of the impact that the commander's conduct makes on his subordinates. So if he refers to enemy forces in a derogatory or dismissive way, then he can expect his subordinates to receive a message through that, that he thinks of them in a derogatory and dismissive way, and that is likely to affect the way they in turn treat those enemy forces. So whilst I'm not saying that it, in my experience, that it is taught in military academies how you refer to military -- to enemy forces. What -- what is taught and discussed, as we discussed yesterday, is what we -- what I've described as command climate, which is the impact that every action of the commander makes on his subordinates. The sort of language and the views he takes and the opinions he expresses, as I said yesterday, is all part of that formation of the command climate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then, on another final topic on this still, the same document, in reference to paragraph number 5, it says in three sentences: "While the task is being completed, the Main Staff, artillery and rocket regiment, shall provide artillery support to the best their ability (ammunition availability.) I am sending Mr. Miro Colic from the Main Staff POVRS officer with whom you can discuss the possibility of using the Maljutka and TF8 FAGOT systems. " Forgive my pronunciation, if I said those wrongly. Then: "Air support will continue to be provided, as agreed by Mr. Miro Lovric, Chief of the Main Staff, Air Force." Now, in each of those references, there is a reference General Petkovic to certain actions being taken or approved or services provided by, if you will, the Main Staff. Can you comment on the significance or whether in some issues -- some instances the Main Staff itself can directly control certain assets or make certain operative decisions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, it's quite normal in the military organisations for either scarce assets or perhaps assets with long range, such as these rocket launchers and air, to be held centrally at a high level rather than penny-packeted out to lower levels. In that way the commander retains flexibility and can reinforce wherever he wants, whenever he wants, according to the circumstances. So, in this case, I would read this to mean that the rocket regiment has been held centrally and is allocated and controlled from the Main Staff, and that is what it's referring to and why, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on using the terminology of assuming, and the Chamber will draw upon the evidence that it has heard to date, but as you mentioned a moment ago, I'm just looking back at your answer just now on line 13, you said, "for either scarce assets or perhaps assets with long range," et cetera. Assuming that the heavier - I'm using the terminology heavier weapons, such as perhaps tanks, larger artillery; that is, artillery other than typical kinds of infantry support weapons, small calibre mortars - if in the HVO, heavier weaponry was, if you will, a scarce or precious commodity, would that reinforce your view that these would be then more likely to be controlled by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this. It calls for speculation. Where is the factual basis? He's asking him to speculate. These may be important assets, but here we're going about concrete military equipment, and he's trying to get the gentleman to divine from this particular -- these particular passages as to whether other major assets were being controlled by the Main Staff. Now, I don't represent the Main Staff, but I am offended as a lawyer sitting here asking a witness to speculate. Now, if he can show the document, then it can be tied in; but it's purely speculative at this point. Now, the general has given us an answer from which the Trial Chamber can discern whether these assets were scarce and, therefore, perhaps, if there's some sort of factual basis, it can be tied in. But without any factual basis, we're asking for circumstantial evidence based on speculation. I think it's clearly objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If I can respond briefly. Yesterday - and I think quite correctly after I further ultimately understood what was being said; and I was slow on the uptake, perhaps, and I apologise for that - on the question of assuming, and that's why I led off this morning, this is an expert witness. I put to him not, not speculating but assuming, and the Chamber will recall and will know the evidence in the case and decide whether the facts -- whether the facts fit or not. But assuming that these were scarce or precious commodities, I simply asked the general in reference to this document, and there will be at least one more similar document, to indicate a view on whether that would reinforce his view that such assets in those circumstances would be more likely to be controlled at a senior level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I perfectly understand the nature of asking hypothetical questions; and, yesterday, in the context in which it was asked, and in which Judge Trechsel invited the parties to consider as a mode of going forward, was perfectly proper. In my opinion, a hypothetical has to be framed in such a way that either the facts are already in or there is a good faith basis that the facts will be in. But you simply cannot ask hypotheticals where there are not facts in evidence or there's no good faith basis in order to tie it in, because that's the purpose of asking the hypothetical. Now, unless there's a good faith basis on the part of Mr. Scott that's going to tie it in somehow, or it has already been tied in, fine; otherwise, I don't think that the gentleman can answer the question. I have no problem with him being asked hypothetical questions as long as the facts are based on -- or the hypothetical, that is, that based on facts already in evidence or facts that will be in evidence, but not facts that are fanciful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I make a separate point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It will tie it together, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can get perhaps a step further if we lift the issue to a more general level. You are an expert on doctrine, on how battles are conducted, how troops are led. Can you tell the Chamber whether it is a general rule applied in all armies, that the lower you get in firepower, the more in quantity you have; and that always the heavy stuff like air force, heavy weapons, are relatively a scarce commodity. How -- are there general rules on how the command will deal with these, irrespective of whether it be in Africa, in Europe, or wherever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, every army organises itself as it wishes. But in my experience, scarce assets and, as I've said, assets with long range, it is very common to find those held centrally at a high level where the commander can allocate them with much greater flexibility than had they been allocated to lower levels. He does that so he can provide reinforcement in firepower over and above what a particular formation might be able to produce for itself, and he can apply is the military is called main effort. In other words, if his main concentration is in a particular area, he can reinforce that area with as much long range or scarce asset firepower as he himself controls at his own level. If it had been sub-allocated, he wouldn't have been able to do that. Now, in this case, in this case, what is written in this order is that General Petkovic is sending, in the first instance, an officer called Mr. Miro Colic from the Main Staff anti-armour multiple rocket system branch, with whom you can discuss the possibility of using the Maljutka, TF8 FAGOT systems. Now, I would assume that is because those systems are held centrally and controlled by Main Staff, and that is why a Main Staff officer, with specific responsibility for those systems, has been sent forward to discuss it, in exactly the same way "air support," it reads, "will continue to be provided as agreed by Mr. Miro Lovric, Chief of Main Staff, Air Force." Now, it would indicate to me that the air force is being controlled by a branch in the Main Staff for the reasons I have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stewart, I'm sorry that I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was just going to comment that whatever questions Mr. Scott is able to ask, that he does take a little bit more care in the phrasing of the views he attributes to the witness, because we got -- and as it happens, Your Honour Judge Trechsel's questions have really gone specifically and very helpfully to this point. But, quite normally, military organisations for assets to be held centrally at a high level became, that it was more likely, it became the witnesses view, that it was more likely to be controlled by Main Staff. I would invite Mr. Scott to take a little bit more care when he's translating a previous answer in to a view that he puts the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: He will be sure to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has not answered my fellow Judge's question. We clearly understand that resources may be controlled by the Main Staff. But know if we talk about tanks, assuming that the number of tanks is limited - you're not talking about hundreds or thousands of tanks; you're talking about only a few tanks - in your opinion, would the use of tanks in such a case come under the Main Staff, the commander of the operation zone, the commander of the local brigade who normally is in charge of these tanks? In what chain of command is that controlled? Who, talking about these tanks, will make the decisions? Can these decisions be made at the level of the Main Staff, of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't got in front of me an organisation chart of how the HVO formations and units were arranged. If I did have, I could answer your question very specifically, so I will have to answer it on the basis of hypothesis. And to put it in context, the HVO were not very well equipped with heavy weaponry, tanks, rocket systems, et cetera. Under those circumstances, where ad hoc formations are being formed, I would expect it to be sensible for the higher commander to keep those, let's call them, heavy assets centralised and under his immediate command where he can allocate them as necessary. So if, for example, there were but a few tanks where you can put any number on but a few, but let's say 30, as opposed to several battalions or regiments of tanks of 50 or 60 tanks each, that would be normal in a -- a normal Western military organisation. If you, let's say, hypothetically you've only got 30 tanks, then you may sub-allocate them if you see fit, or you may hold them centrally, or you may sub-allocate some and hold some back in reserve. You know, those are all hypothetical answers to a hypothetical question, but the concept of holding scarce assets at a centralised high level is perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I achieved only a very modest rank of lieutenant of infantry, in the reserve of course, when I served in the Hungarian army, but really I do not feel that we have a problem here. Anybody knows that there are special units which are attached to, let's say, a regiment level or other major level which the army has at its disposal. So, therefore, I do not see here the problem. No doubt that the -- the Chief of Staff or his deputy has the power to allocate troops here and there and then to send them; and, of course, on the battlefield that is a special responsibility of the commander who is there, let's say, a commander of the regiment or whatever, battalions, et cetera. So I'm sorry to take the floor now, but I really feel that sometimes we blow-up certain problems which are not really problems as such. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Judge Prandler is perfectly right, but let's complete the discussion on that point. When resources are requested at the Main Staff or from the Main Staff, should that be done through a written document or orally for the higher command to provide officially air support or something else? Should there be official communication between the requesting level of command and the level where such things are decided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and those communications can be in a variety of ways. They could be transmitted by radio or fax or courier, or they could be transmitted in the written word, rather depending on whether it is a pre-planned operation or a current operation that is running very quickly. I would -- I would expect a forward commander, who is requesting tank support in an ongoing battle, to simply call for it on the radio to the higher headquarters, and he would be informed by the higher headquarters as to whether it was available or not and the routes and timings, et cetera, by which it would be arriving. So all, all those mechanisms can be used in a more formal pre-planned operation. One might expect a formal written operation order from the higher headquarters, detailing tasks and resources to the subordinate formations, so that they all know who is getting what, particularly additional resources being allocated from a higher level. So any one or all of these methods could be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could then turn next to Exhibit P 03414, which will be in the second of the binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back -- stepping back now to the question that we ended on yesterday in terms of the use of prisoners or detainees in forced -- in labour. Strike the word "forced" now, just in labour. We'll argue about that later. If I can show you this document from the warden of the Heliodrom, Mr. Stanko Bozic, being sent to, among others, Mr. Valentin Coric, Mr. Berislav Pusic. This report says that: "On the 12th of July, 1993, with the approval of the officer for control of the military police, Mr. Berislav Pusic, 40 detainees were given for work." He goes on to say: "On returning from work, the same military policemen informed us that detainee, Mili Isailovic, has been wounded by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, continuing on, again, the discussion we had had yesterday, about using prisoners in dangerous conditions, et cetera, can you tell us how a responsible commander could be expected or should act on receiving such information, that a prisoner or detainee who has been used in labour has been wounded by opposition forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I any there are various issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to say that, as opposed to the case of the document that we had before us yesterday, this document clearly mentions or refers to the word -- uses the word "detainees," so there's no confusion as to whether we're talking about prisoners, POWs, or detainees. When such a question is put to the witness, I think it should be put to him precisely, because if we're dealing with detainees, they could be detained HVO members and not members of enemy forces. So we should have both these ideas in mind. If it's one's own soldier, can we use such soldier for work purposes. I think that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. Mr. Scott, the word "detainee" that we see in this document may refer to various things. It may refer to HVO detainees, to regular prisoners who happened to be here. These might be people who are serving a sentence after being convicted by the relevant military judiciary. We might be talking about prisoners of war or civilians. We don't know. This should be taken into account. Please proceed, keeping that in mind. But I see that Mr. Pusic's lawyer wants to take the floor, since this document was sent to Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to add something. Given what Mr. Scott said about Mr. Pusic's position, it seems that, on the 12th of July, he was doing something quite different from what is stated in the indictment. If we have a look at paragraph 13, 14, we can see that Mr. Pusic, on the 5th of July, 1993, was involved in other things, and he wasn't an officer for the controlled military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm forced at this point to respond to a number of aspects of what's happening here. Number one, again, what the evidence is and the arguments and the inferences and conclusions to be drawn from the evidence will, of course, be what all the parties will have to discuss in their closing written and oral submissions. Now we're getting into arguments about what the evidence is or isn't, and what the evidence does or does not mean. Now, the document -- if I use the word "prisoner" loosely, I'll try not to do that. Everyone in the courtroom has the document in front of them. Everyone knows that it says repeatedly detainees, 40 detainees et cetera, et cetera. Now, I have to observe, at this point, that we're almost 40 minutes into the first session; and, by now, I've had actually about five minutes of time. So we are really approaching a situation where I don't even know if I will finish my direct examination today. If I only get five minutes in 40, we will not be able to do that. So I just simply make that observation to the Chamber. There will be -- there is time for cross-examination to ask these kinds of question; that is, of course, allowing that there is enough time left for cross-examination when the direct examination is concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you, sir, going back to it, I don't know if you remember. I'm just going to start all over, again, I'm afraid. I put this document in front you, and I asked you: How would a responsible commander react to receiving this information, that a detainee, while being used in work, had been wounded by opposition forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in accordance with the doctrine that we were referring to yesterday, a responsible commander, receiving this report from the central military remand prison, would raise a number of questions. He would note that 40 detainees were given for work; no question of volunteering or being asked there. He would note that they were under military escort, and he would note that one of them had been wounded and been taken to hospital. Therefore, he would probably assume that the work they were being given to do was at least in a place where they were vulnerable to enemy fire, or at least fire from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And, in all that, he would ask himself, Is this in transgression of the laws of armed conflict? And if I consider that it is, I better do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can we then go on to -- excuse me one moment. If we could then go on to Exhibit 4792, P 04792. My apology. Let me catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in this order by Zarko Tole, on the 4th of September, 1993, given to the North-west Herzegovina operative zone - that would be the zone commanded by Mr. Siljeg - he says: "1. Tomorrow, 5 September 1993, stop all movement of UN, UNHCR, and UNPROFOR at the military police check-points in your area of responsibility." Paragraph number 2 goes on to say: "This is to be carried out so as to look as if it was the result of the arbitrary behaviour of the check-point policemen, while we should appear as doing everything to let them get through." Now, can you tell to the Judges, again in terms of command climate, maintaining discipline and order in units, et cetera, what is the effect on subordinate troops when the commander -- when a commander would give that kind of an order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it would be fairly clear to a recipient of this order that, first of all, the issuer of this order is ordering all movements of UN, UNHCR, and UNPROFOR to be prevented, which he would know would be in contravention of the UN agreement. But he would be particularly interested in para 2, where there is obviously an element of deception and deceit coming into it, and he would probably be asking himself, Well, I wonder why we're doing this and what we're help to be preventing the UN from seeing. It's obviously something is going on between the time we've got to stop all movement tomorrow until 1500 when we can let it go again, and he'd be asking himself the question, Well, I wonder what on earth is going on? Is there something nasty and illegal happening? Perhaps he might ask himself. He would, therefore, draw the conclusion that the issuer of the order was potentially conniving in something that he certainly did not want the United Nations to see, and he might, therefore, ask himself, Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we -- in the interest of time, if we could just touch upon -- go quickly forward and touch upon paragraph 55. You're moving on to, again, talking about principles -- the application of principles of command and control, but you mention in paragraph 55, and some of the following paragraphs in particular, the support of staff, the staff function. If I can just point out one particular or two sentences at paragraph 55 in the middle, it says: "The staff has no authority by itself. It derives authority from the commander and only exercises it in his name. Thus, all the activities of the staff are undertaken on behalf of the commander." Perhaps you could just comment briefly on that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is highlighting the authority vested in the commander. It is the commander who has the authority to issue orders to his subordinates; and in order to help in the execution and the organisation of those orders, he has a staff to assist him. The staff issues orders on behalf of the commander, not in its own right. Put another way, the commander has full authority and carries full responsibility and is assisted by his staff in the execution of his commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based upon the research you've done and your overall knowledge and experience of these matters, can you say whether that basic principle or practice applied to the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I've read, the HVO Main Staff applied those principles in the traditional manner, with the staff supporting the commander in executing his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the commander in this instance being the top military commander, and, again, perhaps we can assume or perhaps the Judges know by now, during 1993, that being primarily either Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Praljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go forward, please, to Exhibit P 00502.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I briefly interrupt, Mr. Scott. In the documentation that we have and what we hear, the generals that are here accused today are holding the title of Chief of the General Staff. Now, the Chief of the General Staff is part of the staff. He is not normally the commander. The Commander-in-Chief of the HVO, we heard many times, was Mate Boban. Are you aware of this, and how can you associate this, link this, to what you have just told us according to which these generals were the commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware that there are potential confusions and difficulties in the titles: Chief of the Main Staff, Chief of Staff, Supreme Commander. I believe that those titles were used in different ways at different times to describe different functions. The traditional title "Chief of Staff" would be the chief of the commander's staff. That's the traditional title and the traditional way of understanding it. However, in the UK, for example, the Chief of the General Staff is the head of the army, so -- and sometimes commanders are known as Chiefs of Staff. So who was doing what under what title at what time, I think, bears examination from the facts, rather from -- rather than from perhaps the title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could -- I think we were about to turn to Exhibit 502.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a document that appears to have gone out over the name of Bruno Stojic as head of the HVO defence department. I note, at the beginning, when one compares the English translation to the original document, the date has been -- there's a mistake in the date. It's not the 18th of September, 1993. It's the 18th of September, 1992. It says over the name of Mr. Stojic: "Pursuant to the provisions of Article 1 of the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I issue a short-term formation of the General Staff HVO, effective immediately." Now, can you just briefly look through that document, and of course you've seen it before. What kind of a document is this and what is it doing? What is the function of this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what would be described as a staff table of the headquarters, which line by line delineates each appointment in the headquarters, starting with the chief and going through every member of that headquarters down to including clerk. So it's a comprehensive staff table of every position in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I note as well, just in passing, before we move on past the document, that in the chart, we move across the column from left to right. If you get to column number 11, you say that a rank is linked to - not in every instance but in most instances, in many instances - a rank is then connected to that particular post. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can, in light of this document, ask you to turn to Exhibit P 01683.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you have that, sir, can you tell us what has and how that document, if at all, that kind of document would relate at all to the one we were just looking at. Let me rephrase my question. Is this a further, then, breakdown of the actual names of staffs, persons on the positions -- in positions related to the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This appears to be a list of officers on the Main Staff. Whether it's all officers, I can't be certain. But it's certainly some officers on the Main Staff with their appointment or job and their name, which ties back into the document we were just looking at previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just to follow up on Judge Trechsel's comment, we can see even here that in item number 1, in reference to Milivoj Petkovic, the term that is being used in a document over the name of Mr. Petkovic himself is "Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO," at least as of March 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to the discussion we were having earlier today about certain Main Staff assets, do you see, for example, in item number 16 on the -- on the Main Staff, you have the chief of artillery.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's on the second document. Yes, I do. Chief of artillery, Marko Stojcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then you have later on number 19, the chief of the artillery rocket unit. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. Yes, Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you look at 34 and 35, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, 34 and 35 of what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Turn over the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you seen this document before or is this the first time you're seeing it today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. Well, in this list of the members of staff, there are two officers who apparently belong to a different staff [as interpreted]. Is it common in armies for this possibility of an outside officer coming in to a Main Staff? Is that surprising to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, a correction. There is a correction in the translation. It said coming from, at line 24, a different state, not a different staff. Different state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Officers from a different state, not a different staff. A different state. Miro Prce, an officer of the HV, the Croatian army; Josip Speranca, an officer of the Croatian army. Is it common in staffs to see temporary addition of officers coming from a different army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's very common, particularly when the headquarters is dealing very closely with the nation represented by, in this case, officers of HV. I would take those to be Croatian army liaison officers, in exactly the same way as, for example, when I was Director of Operations, Chief of Staff at the permanent joint headquarters, we had officers from the American SANCOM [phoen] Headquarters, the Dutch headquarters, the French headquarters. So it speeds up the link back to those countries. The fact that there are two HV officers in the -- attached temporarily to the General Staff - they obviously don't appear on the General Staff's staff table because they're not HVO officers - would be a clear indication to me that that headquarters has direct communications and dealings with the HV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can then move on, please, to Exhibit P 04131.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on in terms of the command structure of the HVO, and now we're looking at a document the 12th of August, 1993, issued over the -- at least the typed name and stamp of Slobodan Praljak. It indicates that: "Pursuant to the provisions of the HZ HB armed forces, defence forces, Official Gazette," et cetera, "I hereby order: "The GS Main Staff of the armed forces, or defence forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, shall be directly subordinated to the Supreme Commander of the HZ HB armed forces. "The General Staff exerts direct command over the operative zones, south-east, north-east, central," et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just stopping, pausing there, is that not an uncommon form of military organisation where you have again the very top military commander or commanders and then military districts or military zones directly subordinated to the senior command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I find nothing training in that. That is simply laying out the chain of command from the Supreme Commander through the Main Staff down to the operative zones. That's unity of command as professed in the doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then continuing on, and touching once again on one of the topics of this morning, it also says that the General Staff has: "Direct command over professional units, the Bruno Busic, the Ludvig Pavlovic regiments." Do you have any knowledge or experience on -- based on your military career that, in addition to such things as artillery or rocket forces or air force, there may be certain specialised units or profession -- the terminology of "professional units" that may be directly commanded by central high command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whilst I have no knowledge of what the Bruno Busic and the Ludvig Pavlovic Regiments are, I can readily equate this to, for example, special forces being held centrally under command of the highest headquarters, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the interest of time we'll just go through this very quickly. I just mention in passing, because the Chamber will have heard evidence in recent weeks, for example, about the logistics, the main logistics centre in Grude, which is referenced in paragraphs 3 through -- well, paragraph 3 in particular. Then if I can direct your attention to item 6, General Praljak's order says: "I strictly prohibit any violation of the command system as regulated by this order in the Herceg-Bosna armed forces. I hereby designate the commanders directly subordinated to me and the individual organs of the HVO Main Staff responsible for the consistent execution of this order." Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is simply stressing that there is one chain of command, and that is the chain of command designated in this order. In other words, Supreme Commander, Main Staff, operative zones, and that's the chain of command that should function at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I listened to you, and it's a bit difficult for me. You talk about the chain of command at line 18 of page 25. You talk about the Supreme Command, the Main Staff, and the commander of the operational zones. As far as I understood earlier on, the Main Staff does not have responsibilities when there is a Supreme Command that is in operation. Can you perhaps elucidate that? In this chain of command, what does the Main Staff do? Is it below or alongside the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Main Staff supports the top military commander, and the top military commander is subordinate in turn to the Supreme Commander. Now, I understand that there is also some difficulty in the nomenclature here that Supreme Commander, in accordance with other documents, could well be the president himself. So the president -- the chain of command goes from the president through the top military commander supported by his Main Staff down to the operative zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I've understood you properly, Mate Boban is the Supreme Commander; and below him, there is the person who issued this order, Major General Slobodan Praljak; and below that, there are the commanders of the operational zones. Is that the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the chain of command as I understand it from this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That would mean, to get it exactly precisely, where it says "General Staff," one must understand Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think one understands -- I'm not sure what his exact title is. But chief of the Main Staff is not the Chief of Staff of the headquarters, but chief of the Main Staff is, let's call him, the top military commander, General Praljak. In his staff, he would have a chief of staff with some slightly different title. It is a bit confusing, but that's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and excuse me, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. If I can just briefly comment. I do understand the Chamber's questions. But I have to say, at this point, some of the confusion is a result of the historical language. It wasn't, of course, the Prosecution that chose the titles that were used and the terminology that was used. Of course, the Chamber will have a large, as it already does, a large amount of documentation in fronts of it to -- to ultimately make those determinations. But to the extent that that language is not documents, we can't change that. There was a terminology change in mid-1993 in which they -- what had been the chief of the Main Staff was then termed to be the commander of the HVO armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has not been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it hasn't been alleged today at all that any of this confusion regarding nomenclature is the fault of the Prosecution. There is no need for a defensive position here. No allegation has been made against my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning to you. I have an objection to make with respect to the way in which the Prosecution has prepared the witness; that is to say, they have not prepared him with the documents at his disposal. Now, Supreme Commander, commander. Somebody is just dancing and here, and it's up to the Prosecution. The Prosecution has had access to all the documents, to look at the transformations that the HVO went through. So the witness should have been presented with documents to show all this, not to have to discuss whether it was Tole, Petkovic, Praljak who was Chief of Staff or who was Chief of Staff. So it's not the witness's fault for not having been provided the documents on time and showing the different structural changes and organisational changes along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, to briefly respond, my point -- the point of the comment that I made a moment ago, and I appreciate counsel's comment. I wasn't trying to be personally defensive. I was just trying to further assist the Chamber in the state of affairs on this one. Also, if I was defending anyone, I was defending perhaps the witness because it's not the witness's choice of language that we're dealing with. It's the choice of language in the documents. As Mr. Petkovic well knows, from having been involved in this system, those are the words that are found in the documents, I can assure you that if you go through documents, you will see Supreme Commander used in name of different ways. We have had these conversations since April 1996 with a number of witnesses. So, the Chamber, of course, assisted by all the evidence and assisted by this witness as much as possible, will ultimately, of course, have to make those determinations, with hopefully the assistance of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to turn in your binder to 1D 01246, at the end of the second binder, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not there. Say the number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. 1 D -- it's a bit different nomenclature, but 1D 01246. It may be the last document in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is indeed the last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just continuing on, sir, we've proceeded in this particular respect largely chronologically, by showing you a number of command documents from earlier in 1993 to the middle of August 1993 of different commanders, both during the time when Mr. Petkovic was the top commander, the time when Mr. Praljak was the top commander, and now by the middle of November, 1993, the top commander has become Ante Roso. Tying back some of these things to issue of command climate and control of troops and discipline, I would ask you to look at the third paragraph of the document in particular. And I should say at the top, it says "To all units," "To all units and members of the Croatian Defence Council." "Subject: Warning," third paragraph, "Because of the historical responsibility before our own nation, we are determined to immediately punish any act of murder of civilians, elderly people, women, children, arson and looting, rape, and other acts of violence against people and their property within execution by firing squad." Now, can you comment on not only that document -- that paragraph, but to the extent that you've been able to scan the document in toto, can you comment on that order as an instance of exercising command and establishing command climate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, any recipient of this document would realise that they now have a commander in command who takes a very strong view on the sort of barbarities described in chapter 3, and goes on to say that - I assume it's shorthand and rhetoric and it's within the military manuals of law and et cetera, et cetera - but if convicted, anybody found guilty of those offences will be executed by firing squad. I assume that that was allowed for. It goes on to say: "The crimes and genocide perpetrated by the Muslim terrorists against Croats do not give us the right to respond in kind. The future Croat generations must not be ashamed of their fathers' inhumane conducts." Here is a commander who is getting a very tight grip of barbaric behaviour and making certain that everybody knows what his view is. He's addressed this order it all units. And, lastly, going back to discussions we had yesterday, giving the order is easy part. Making it happen is more difficult. One would expect - I have no knowledge of it - but one would expect this commander, Ante Roso, to have followed that up vigorously, if there were instances of the sort of thing that he is drawing everybody's attention to, that he will simply not tolerate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The very last sentence, just before we move on, says: "This warning must be read in front of the formations." Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that's a nice example of the first instance of making it happen. So if every soldier is going to have had this read to him by his immediate commander, in the first instance, General Roso could at least be satisfied that his message has got down to the very lowest level, and that everybody knows what his position is. After that, it's up to General Roso to make sure his position is carried through in the event that any instances of the sort mentioned here actually happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to a series of paragraphs in general, starting with paragraph 58. I'm not going to have time to discuss much of that, but I do want to ask you about one topic on this, because the Chamber has heard other evidence touching on some of these things. From the perspective of a military commander, what information, such as media reports, reports on the television, reports on radio, reports in newspapers, open sources, what sort of role does that information play in the information being received by a commander and how does a commander deal with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander will receive information from what is described as all sources. He will receive reports and information coming up the traditional military chain of command. He will receive information from his own staff officers visiting forward to units and reporting back. He will receive knowledge from his own visits. In addition to that, in today's world, all commanders will be very conscious of the media, the pervasive nature of the media. It is not uncommon, for example, if you go into military headquarters, to find CNN and BBC World playing on the wall. That is very much part of life today, and it is part of the -- it forms part of the sources of information that a commander and his staff would be receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Taking one further example of that, assuming, assuming for the moment, that this same information had not have been received by the commander up his own chain of command, for whatever reason, but assuming that an atrocity or some issue -- some event in Bosnia was reported in a Zagreb newspaper and that information came to the information of the commander, what would be the responsibility of the commander on hearing that information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very least, the commander would start asking questions and -- and institute an investigation into the veracity of that report. I say "would." Should.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can then move on to paragraph 62. In that paragraph, I think, for the first time in your report, General, you introduce a concept that you call "two up and two down." Could you please explain that briefly to us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Starting with the notion of "two down," commanders think two down in order that when they -- when they issue tasks and allocate resources, they're doing so with a fundamental understanding of what is required, and I think I gave an example. Yes. So if a brigade commander, for example, is -- has a number of battalions, one of which has taken serious casualties and it only has two of its four companies operational, then he by thinking two levels down from brigade, battalion, company, then he would realise that that battalion is only half as capable perhaps as the other battalions, and, therefore, he would give them different and lesser tasks than the other battalions. Thinking "two up" is all about commanders understanding where they are in the wider course of events. What is their higher commander's intent, what is it he's trying to achieve, and what role in it he has to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. General, I think we'll have to move on, then, to paragraph 66; and starting in that part of your report, you're discussing more specifically military discipline. You say at the beginning of paragraph 66, you say: "Military discipline is codified to ensure that soldiers operate in active operations in a disciplined and effective manner." And if I could -- and you reference in that paragraph, among others, Exhibit P 00301, so if we could please go to Exhibit 301.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe Mr. President, if I'm not mistaken, this is the document that you raised earlier today, and I believe -- I have some indications that there is in fact a better version of the document available, which I would certainly provide to the parties and the Chamber, Your Honour. I believe it's actually marked as Exhibit P 00425. It's a better copy of the same document. It's not in the binders because I'm just responding to the Chamber's -- to the President's inquiry or point, and we can take further steps on that. We will have to work with 301 at least for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In -- in conducting your work, sir, did you have a chance to -- well, you've cited in your report, so I suppose the answer is obvious, but you had an opportunity to review and consider the content of Exhibit 301?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what kind of a comment -- what comment can you make in terms of the quality of this document at least as a document? Is it the sort of a codification of military discipline that you would expect?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a comprehensive document. I think it has 112 articles in it, covering a wide range of subjects, which, taken together, would create the disciplinary parameters within which the HZ HB military forces would be required by law to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. MR. SCOTT Could I ask then to also then turn to Exhibit P 00282. It should be reasonably close by, a few exhibits earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that document, this says: "Excerpt from the rules on military discipline." How does that document compare -- or what role does that document play in setting out further a disciplinary system, if you will?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read this to be a sort of abbreviated aide-memoire, concentrating attention on the essentials, and it rather harks back to what we were talking about yesterday, in terms of the HVO was being set up and conducting a war all at the same time. The previous article was 112 -- the previous document was 112 articles long, extremely complicated and detailed. But an officer receiving this rather succinct four-page document could quickly read this and grasp the essentials of -- of discipline and the disciplinary code he was required to basis actions on. So it's a helpful aide-memoire, resume of the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just as an example, on at least on page 2 of the English version, one of the things set out is which disciplinary measures may can be taken, ranging from warning, to caution, to confinement to barracks, to military detention. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps, we can just finish on this before the break. You then, having those documents in mind, in paragraph 67, at about the middle of the paragraph, you give the example. Well, actually earlier in the paragraph as well, you talk about a sentry who falls asleep on watch. You say, in the middle of that paragraph, and you go on to say: "But a soldier who falls asleep on watch on training is likely to be severely punished simply because he must realise the seriousness of his actions if he conducts himself like that on active operations." Can you comment further?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the -- when the military undergo training, they train as for war and they make it as realistic as possible. Sleeping on sentry, as an example, is a very, very serious offence either on exercise or on operations: On operations, for obvious reasons; but on exercise to impress on all the seriousness of the offence. Whether it -- whether it be in peace or war, it is -- one is operating under the same legal code; although, that said, in wartime there may be some extra provisions added on top of -- of the code. But, basically, military discipline is the same in peace as it is in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you. Perhaps you can assist us a bit further. When you say in your report "severely punished," let's take both situations, and we'll draw on the British Army. If that happened in the British Army, a soldier who was on sentry duty during a training exercise, a training exercise, fell asleep, was found to have fallen asleep at his post, what would be the disciplinary action that would be taken?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known soldiers who have fallen asleep on sentry be charged, and, when found guilty, committed to gaol for 28 days, which is the maximum a commander officer at that time could give. And, interestingly, in the document we just noted, I see that the HVO had a 30-day detention. That was not uncommon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I change that scenario to that same conduct occurred in actual wartime conditions, would that change or what would the punishment likely be in that situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The punishment would be -- well, that would be up to the court to decide, but what is usual is that a commanding officer has a limitation on the level of punishment that he can issue to convicted -- guilty soldiers. If he was not satisfied that that punishment met the crime, then he could refer the -- the accused to a higher court or a court-martial, where heavier sentences were -- were available. So it would be up to the commander to -- to decide how to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Chamber will allow me just to hopefully finish on this point before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it -- you just said something just now. I want to be accurate. The punishment, well, it's translated here, in line 13, that the punishment met the crime, or it might have been fit the crime, but that's my question. In military justice or military discipline is there generally a concept that the punishment should fit the crime?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if a soldier falling asleep on duty would warrant being thrown in the brig for 28 days, what kind of punishment could be expected in connection with the severe mistreatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first instance, the severe mistreatment of civilians is -- would be contrary to the laws of armed conflict, and it is probably, therefore, most certainly well beyond anything that the local commander could deal with. So, in the first instance, that soldier would be arraigned before his commanding officer, and the commanding officer would then refer it to a -- a higher court, if I can put it like that, a court-martial, where sentences are Draconianly heavier if found guilty or the availability of much heavier sentences is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And while that he process is playing out, would that particular soldier accused of such a severe offence, would he continue to be used in ongoing military operations, for example, where further contact with civilians could be expected?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that would -- that's up to the commander's discretion, really. If this is a soldier who is habitually known to mistreat civilians, then he would probably be remanded in custody, perhaps, or at least removed from the scene where he would have the opportunity to do that. If, on the other hand, you know, everyone is innocent until proven guilty, there is -- there is an element of discretion and decision that a commander must apply there, according to the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question was put in a certain way and a certain answer was given that corresponded to the question. It's clear to me that the expert witness is talking about the situation, I assume, in the British Army. But when you have a look at the entire text, three months later, when someone goes through this, it won't be clear. So, perhaps, my colleague could be more specific and state that it's just an example of how things might work in the British Army, because it's quite obvious that he's not speaking about the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. Witness, for the sake of argument, let's assume that, in the British Army, we have a soldier who is guarding a prison and who mistreats prisoners. What would happen in such a case in your army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, regrettably, we have had some of those instances recently in Iraq, and the accused were brought before their commanding officer and were subsequently committed for trial by court-martial. Not all, I'm happy to say; in fact, very few were found guilty, but the due process of law was seen through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Time has come to take the break. We are going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I understand that Mr. Karnavas wanted to take the floor for three minutes in private session, so we'll stop him at -- we'll stop just before the end of this session, and then you'll have the floor once the witness has left the courtroom. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do apologise to the courtroom. I'm afraid I wasn't watching the clock closely enough. My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to pick up on where we left before the break, I don't want to leave the wrong impression, and, of course, you find yourself sitting in a room full of lawyers and Judges, all of whom are very much, of course, in favour of due process. But, again, I want to make it quite clear, if a commander, faced with a scenario. Let me give you a scenario. The commander has just received a command from one of his subordinate commanders, a junior officer, that information is coming back that civilians in a village are being executed, by any side. I don't care if it's the HVO, the ABiH, the American army, the British Army. And this information comes to the commander's attention. Now, you've talked about invoking the military justice system: Calling the military prosecutor, calling the military police. But what does the commander do on the spot? What does the commander do? Well, I've called the military prosecutor. He'll get here in three months. In the meantime, just go on about your business? I mean, what does the commander do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are commanders at all levels. The commander at the level where this atrocity is being carried out, assuming he's not part of the atrocity himself, would have the perpetrators arrested and would pass them back up the chain of command, where the senior and appropriate commander would decide what they were going to do with him. If it was a clear case of, let's say for the example, you know, burning houses and raping women or something, then one would expect the perpetrators to be brought before the justice system very quickly, remanded in gaol, so that they couldn't do that again, and would -- and due process would then -- would then click in. They would then be brought before the senior commander who is permitted to deal with them. He -- he would hear the evidence. He would decide whether he could deal with them or whether it should be passed to a higher level, a higher court, and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I apologise to Mr. Scott, too, but could we clarify something? With regard to the hypothetical situation, does it concern the killing of civilians in a village that is being defended or a village that is not being defended? And in such a hypothetical situation, are we dealing with the killings of civilians linked to some sort of military events or not? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that be left, please, for cross-examination so that I can continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on to paragraph 68, continuing to talk about discipline, in the second sentence, you say: "If a commander is seen not to impose discipline when disciplinary action is called for, then he will be regarded as weak, or conniving, or both." And can you comment on that further, and in particular, can you comment on when you say "or conniving," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in an army that is signed up to the international laws of armed conflict - as mine has and as the HVO had, it would appear - everybody would know that they were expected to conduct themselves in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and laws of armed conflict; and, in particular, they would know or they should know that certain very obvious crimes are not tolerated and are against the law, such as barbarity to civilians, shooting prisoners, the sort of thing that we've been talking about. Now, if those actions are being perpetrated and the chain of command is taking no action, then that sends a very clear message to both the perpetrators and the observers, that this sort of behaviour is acceptable. I've used the words, "the commander will be regarded either as weak," in other words, he's not confident or strong enough to take action for whatever reason; "or conniving," by which I mean that he does not disapprove of the actions, in fact may even approve of the action. But, in any way, he is complicit in it because knowing that these actions are taking place, he is not taking -- he is not taking action as he is required to do, in accordance with his own doctrine, to bring the perpetrators to - what's the word am I looking for? - to account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With these -- some of these questions in mind, if we could then turn next to P 00856.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This appears to be an order issued again by, or at least over the name of Mr. Petkovic, on the 4th of December, 1992. Can you just -- this appears to be an order to establish, I'll say generally, public order or to control the discipline of troops. Can you just look at that and comment on that as an order, in terms of trying -- regaining control over unsoldierly -- in the first paragraph, it says "unsoldierly behaviour, demolishing facilities," et cetera, and comment on this as an attempt to gain control over that situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order that is presumably based on a concern that off-duty soldiers are remaining armed, many of them becoming under the influence of alcohol and getting quite out of control as a result. And in the light of that, the commander, Petkovic, has issued an order to subordinate units, detailing how he hopes this can be avoided in future, laying down procedures for handing in weapons before off-duty soldiers go off to the cafes, and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having said that, I'll return once again to: Giving the order is the easy part. Making it happen is more difficult. This would have to be followed through, and, indeed, there is an attempt to put into position a reporting system, which is part of following through. But I would -- I would expect this commander to eyeball his subordinate commanders and poke them in the chest and impress on them, you know, that he thought it was important and they ought to get a grip of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. That last comment, to some extent, perhaps not physically poking them in the chest, maybe he did; but in number 1, at least somewhat figuratively, is it fair to say he is first off starting by saying, all commanders and assistants are obligated to essentially get control of the situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What he's saying here is as commanders, each and every commander in the chain of command, that is, down to the lowest level, section commander, should be explaining to their men the consequences of this sort of actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then, in reference to such things as the code of military discipline that we were referring to before the break is item number 4: "Commanders are obligated to finally start taking measures regulated by the disciplinary code." So at the level of disciplinary measures available to the more local commanders, I mean, can you give us some ideas of the kind of disciplinary measures that would be available to the local commander to address this situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when reviewing one of the earlier documents, you pointed to a number of tabulated measures which range from fairly mild, confining to barracks, then there would be issues like additional work, you know, metaphorically peeling the potatoes, rather than going out to play, down to the measures of severity to -- to detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just -- you've said a moment ago, you looked ahead - I'll refer you specifically to paragraph number 8 - and you said one of things you would expect an officer to do is then implement a system to monitor, if you will, the implementation of his order, so that the information, the reports are coming back up the chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And those will be being received by the staff and the headquarters periodically and as necessary and appropriate brought to the attention of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we then next go to Exhibit P 02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There's one point that strikes me here. It's in number 6, where the order is to prevent in a most vigorous manner the use of alcohol over Christmas and New Year. Now, is this a realistic general order? Would other armies have a ban on alcohol during holidays?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that that's what it necessarily means. I mean, the -- I read the substance of this order to be about off-duty soldiers carrying weapons, combined with the use -- excessive use of alcohol. I'm not sure whether this means Christmas and the New Year has been cancelled this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could then go on to Exhibit P 02036.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you say the number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. P 02036. In other words, 2036. This is, again, an order over the name of Milivoj Petkovic, dated the 22nd of April, 1993. Perhaps, again, you can scan through the six paragraphs of the order and comment on, again, this as an effort to gain control over troops in a particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can be a bit more specific, it may assist everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look particularly at paragraph number 2, in light of some of the conversation we've had so far this morning. Again, Mr. Petkovic in this situation, at the end of paragraph, says: "Render commanders at all levels responsible for the conduct and actions of their soldiers." What -- what is the commander in the position of Mr. Petkovic doing to say render -- make sure the commanders at all levels know that they are responsible for dealing with this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Brigadier Petkovic is obviously facing here a rather difficult situation in that that appears to be a pretty widespread and general breakdown in discipline, and he cites failing to carry out orders, taking their own decisions on the basis of their own judgement, planning conducted their own operations, terrorising civilians, obstructing UNPROFOR, and so forth. This sounds like a force that is almost out of control. In order to try and get it back into control, he's trying to energise the chain of command by reminding commanders at all levels of their responsibilities. I mean, this is a general breakdown in discipline at every level, where commanders at all levels appear to be pretty ineffective. This is obviously worrying to Brigadier Petkovic, who is now trying to get it back into control, and has issued this written order. But this is perfect example where the presence of the commander is now required in a very energetic fashion, as I've said metaphorically, poking the chest of his subordinate commanders, to make sure they get a grip, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, again, in light of some of the discussion this morning about what actions would be -- what immediate or short-term actions would be available to the commander, other than ultimately some military prosecution? I direct your attention to paragraph number 3, and Mr. Petkovic says: "Immediately set about arresting individuals or groups who have gone totally out of control." So he is there, in fact, sanctioning again, at least by this order, the immediate arrest of such persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In fact, he goes further in the next paragraph: "Use all available means, including the means of force, to stop," and here he's citing really serious incidents, "torching and destroying civilian buildings, and whose actions are sheer terrorism." So, yeah, he wants these people brought to account, and he wants them brought to account rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm reading the introduction to the order, where we have the explanation of why he issued this order. Obviously, there was an inspection of the HVO units, and this order is also based on a number of reports that must have been sent by the brigades. That's the reason why he has issued this order. According to you, in such a situation, should he have then made sure that his order had been obeyed; or, as he says at paragraph 6, was it enough to say that he held all levels of command responsible for implementing these tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, paragraph 6 is where it starts. It certainly is not where it ends. Yes. He is right in saying, "I hold levels of command responsible for implementing these tasks," and now he will be taking much interest in seeing how they effectively carry that out.
