And in the event that they're not carrying it out, then taking the necessary actions in terms of removing commanders and replacing them with more effective commanders or whatever is required. So it's not sufficient just to leave it at paragraph 6, and then sit back and relax. If -- if the state of affairs is as serious as this order would suggest, a high-level commander would be extremely energetic in ensuring that it was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could then go to Exhibit P 00679.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I'm sorry for interrupting. My question relates to Exhibit 2036 in the order issued by Brigadier Petkovic. At paragraph 5, we see that he requests energetic measures against any individual obstructing UNPROFOR's activities, as well as the UNHCR and other international institutions or organisations. This draws my attention because I draw a parallel with another document we examined this morning, P 04792, where another one of the Chief of Staff, Zarko Tole, stated at paragraph -- the first paragraph that all movements of the UNHCR and UNPROFOR should be stopped. And at paragraph 2, he says that this should not be seen as a measure coming from the upper echelons. My question to you, based on your experience, is that to me these seem contradictory orders coming, first, from officers working at very high levels in the Main Staff. So we have contradictory messages sent. Does this affect the behaviour of troops on the terrain or the behaviour of lower-level commanders? Could this have an impact on the conduct of operations? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you put your finger on exactly what I was alluding to, when we dealt with the previous document where orders were given to prevent UNPROFOR's freedom of movement, when the recipients of those orders would know that that was contrary to the agreements with the United Nations. I hesitate to use the word"illegal," but it was -- it was an order that they would know was contrary to the agreements. You then compare that with the order we've just seen, which is quite correct, which says that UNPROFOR, et cetera, should be given total freedom of movement. Now, what that means is when you have an officer who is issuing orders that are plainly contrary to either the law or agreements, you are beginning to create a command climate of total confusion, and the soldiers don't know what's right and what's wrong, or what's being enforced and what isn't. That was exactly the point being made on the previous document, where they were had being specifically ordered to prevent UNPROFOR's freedom of movement, and then exacerbated by some sort of deceit and deception cover story as to why they're going to do that until 1500 hours and then let them move on. You put are finger on exactly the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, if I could then ask you to look at P 00679, which, again, is an order over the name of Mr. Petkovic, dated the 31st of October, 1992. Item number 1 says: "We have reports that (Muslim) houses in the municipality of Prozor are being torched and destroyed." And in point number 3, he goes on to say: "These incidents will cause great problems for us because they are writing about this in the foreign media." Now, one of the questions I asked you this morning was the impact of public media, if you want to call it, whatever one: The open source, the newspapers, CNN, what have you. Does this document appear to be that Mr. Petkovic is, in fact, aware of and alert to the problems caused by such reporting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think I missed the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. Can you just comment in terms of the discussion that we had earlier this morning on the role or effect that reports in public media can have upon the conduct of a commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, plainly, the media has focused the attention of Brigadier Petkovic in this event, but the thing I really find striking about this order is notwithstanding the fact that Muslim houses in the municipality of Prozor are being torched and destroyed, notably absent is any form of statement like "in direct contravention to the international laws of armed conflicts and I will not tolerate this," or words to that effect. It is wrapped up in, These incidents are going to cause us great problems because they're appearing in the foreign media. Now, that sends a pretty subtle message, in my view; not that I am particularly -- not that the author, Brigadier Petkovic, is concerned necessarily that Muslim houses are being burnt and torched. What he's concerned about is it's causing him embarrassment and problems, because it's coming to the attention of the media. So this -- this order might have been written in a very much different and much more effective way if it was serious about trying to prevent Muslim houses, in general, being torched. A recipient of this order could easily take the view that, Ah, well, the commander obviously wants us -- if we're going to do this, we've got to make sure the media aren't there and we've got to cover it up. This would be the assumption that could easily be made from such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can then go, jump to paragraph 55 of your report. Excuse me for a moment. I may have made -- sorry, paragraph 72. My apology. Wrong number. It starts about halfway through paragraph 72. You find this part of your report that says: "Responsibility for the action of subordinates follows: An officer is personally liable for violations of the laws of war, 'if he knew or could have known that units subordinate to him or other units or individuals were planning the commission of such violations, and, at a time when it was still possible to prevent their commission, failed to fake measures to prevent such violations.'" And then going on to say: "Personal accountability is also emphasised if an officer, aware that violations of the laws of war have been committed, fails to institute disciplinary or criminal proceedings again the offender, or fails to report the violations to his superior officer." Now, some of those who practice in this institution might find that language to be closely parallel to one of our statutes, but you're here quoting a JNA document, Federal Secretariat for National Defence Regulations from 1988, Exhibit 7, that we were looking at yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as a statement of general principle, and if you compare that to what you might find in the British Army, for example, would you consider that to be pretty common language of that sort about the responsibility of a commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely in accord with -- with the instructions, teaching, doctrine of any army that is duty-bound to abide by the international laws of war. The way it's phrased is extremely good, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I can next direct your attention then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the pause, Your Honour, but I'm trying, because of the time, I'm trying now to read through both the report and my outline to see what we could possibly -- either it's already been covered or, unfortunately, can be skipped at this stage. So I apologise for the pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think, General, I could perhaps next ask you to look at Exhibit P 03019. This, again, appears to be a document issued over the name of Milivoj Petkovic, dated the 30th of June, 1993, which the Judges may remember that particular date and what happens around that time. Just to set the scene, General, if I can direct your attention to paragraph number 8, which in the English version, at least, is at the top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. This document has already been admitted into evidence, and I myself used it a number of times. I don't mind at all analysing the document in a million different ways. However, I'm raising an objection because this time the witness - and in the introduction, it says he doesn't know what the situation was like on the battlefield and what was happening on the territory in 1993 on the territory of Herceg-Bosna, and that is why he cannot testify about the facts - is now being shown a document which cannot be understood unless one is well acquainted with the facts on the ground and the circumstances on the ground in connection which this order was issued. Therefore, if this witness does not know what was going on on the 30th of June, 1993, and if he does not know the conduct of the BH army towards the Muslims in the HVO in the first six months of 1993, then this witness cannot interpret this document in a proper manner, and that is why I object to having the witness comment on these documents without previously establishing whether the witness does, indeed, have the facts at his fingertips, with respect to the situation on the ground in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will decide whether the witness may answer the question or not. Mr. Scott, please put your question to the witness. The witness will answer your question. The Defence will cross-examine if they see fit, and the Judges will draw their own conclusions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to paragraph number 8, it says: "All Muslim soldiers, who are still active in some units, should be disarmed and isolated. "In the places, within the area of responsibility where there is a Muslim population, all military-capable Muslim men should be isolated. Women and children should be left in their houses-apartments." Now, my question to you is not to address whether you know the specific facts that happened at that time; but as a military commander, apart from other things, if this issue was ordered, and assuming that there are thousands of Muslim men in this area, what logistic steps, what logistics issues does this raise when the general of the army, the supreme commander raises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, in order for the witness to be able to answer, he has to be told that the Muslim soldiers are members of HVO units; otherwise, the witness might think that it's the ABiH members that have to be disarmed. He has to be told about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will amended my scenario. I was simply reading the document, but I will amended the document by adding the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, you can -- I don't there will be any dispute in the courtroom, I hope, at this stage that, when it says "all Muslim soldiers who are still active in some units," the reference there "in some units" is in HVO units, "should be disarmed." Of course, in the remaining part of the paragraph, it talks about the Muslim population and the military-capable men, regardless of whether they're in any units of any army or not. Now, the questions I put to you, and assuming that there are thousands or tens of thousands of such persons in this area, were General Petkovic to give this order, what were the logistic implications of implementing and carrying out this order? You said to us there has to be "two up and two down" thinking. What does General Petkovic have to do to expect this order to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this order carries with it a number of implied tasks. Those who are being arrested or detained have presumably got to be taken to somewhere where they will be kept in secure conditions, so they will need transport. They'll need guards. And once in the location to which they are being tank, there will have to be due concern shown for a roof over their heads, food, water, sanitation, and everything like that. Now, I don't know what the numbers are involved are here, but you said assume there are thousands. This is a potentially very serious logistic issue, which -- which would need some preparation in advance to get the witness right; or if there was not time or not the intent to prepare in advance, then it would require a lot of activity after the event to get the conditions right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And, again, because we have to move with some haste at this point, let me just add about another part of the order. Just in terms of chain of command, and in terms of passing a command's orders down from the top to the bottom, so to speak, can I ask you to look at the bottom after Mr. Petkovic's name. Do you see there is a further instruction at the end of that order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We submit this order to the chief of the HVO Main Staff for your information and for its implementation..." That one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. You'll have to be a bit slower for translation.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the is sentence underneath the Petkovic signature block?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Then, there's another block that starts: "Mostar, 30 June 1993." "We submit this order of the chief of the HVO Main Staff for your information and for its implementation," over the name Miljenko Lasic, commander of the south-east operative zone, submitted to 2nd HVO Brigade and 3rd HVO Brigade."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, is that an effective way of transmitting an order from your commander down through your own command? Essentially, is General Lasic, Mr. Lasic saying, I received this order from General Petkovic. I'm now passing it on to you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that instance, it is a thoroughly ineffective way to pass on this order because it details no tasks, it details no logistics support, it details no hows, whys, and wherefores. This is, obviously, going to be an extremely complicated and sensitive operation, which requires the allocation of resources, none of which is mentioned here. The order is simply passed on and the 2nd Brigade and the 3rd Brigade are presumably just left to get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, for instance, following up on what you said earlier, in passing the order down his chain of command, does -- does the Commander Lasic provide any orders, direction, guidance, information as to where the prisoners should be -- detained persons should be taken, how they should be provided for, how their needs should be met, what vehicles will be provided for transporting them to wherever they're going to go? Does Mr. Lasic provide any such information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this document, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I've listened to your answer very carefully. When reading this order, I find that there's a situation deriving from this order. At paragraph 1, there's the request for fortification or enforcement of units. Paragraph 2, 3, 4, all these paragraphs relate to units that are in theatre, in the field. At paragraph 7, we see the problem arise, appear. It is that the ABiH troops have infiltrated some of their men and losses have resulted from this. It seems, but I might be mistaken, it seems that paragraph 8 has to be connected or related to paragraph 7. "This is an emergency situation," we see it mentioned here in this document, "therefore, it is requested that Muslim who are members of the HVO should be isolated," whereas, initially, the order aims at reinforcing the lines. According to you, despite that the main thrust of the order is to reinforce the line and with the information about in the infiltration of the enemy forces in the lines, do you believe in this context that the fact of disarming the Muslim soldiers should have led to an additional order related to logistics and all that? You've mentioned it yourself. Did this not come under the purview of Lasic? Was the operational man in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding, when you combine paragraph 7 with paragraph 8, is that there is plainly concern, understandable concern, since now the HVO are being engaged by ABiH Muslim defence forces, that the Muslim soldiers within the HVO may no longer be reliable. I could understand that. I could, therefore, understand a -- an order to disarm them and isolate them. What I would expect to see after that is some form of -- well, certainly all the logistics considerations of how that's going to happen, where it's going to happen, how they're going to be cared for, looked after, et cetera. I would expect to see at some stage some form of investigative procedure to -- to ascertain whether those Muslim soldiers were a risk or a threat or not. But I stand by what I said previously: If large numbers, for whatever reason, of Muslim soldiers and Muslim males are being rounded up, that is a severe logistic problem that must be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission. I do apologise to my learned friend Mr. Scott, but I have to say that I consider this witness put in military logic to interpret what was behind the order and point 8 of that order. I think we should explain to the witness briefly what happened on the 30th of June, 1993. What happened was the following, the situation was as follows, General Pringle: The area of part of Mostar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you're going to be taking time now. Perhaps you could do this during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the hour available at my disposal, I won't be able to go through all the areas where my client's name is mentioned. But I think that in just a couple of sentences we can say that on the 30th of June, the HVO lost control over a certain portion, key portions of Mostar and to the north of Mostar, thanks to the treachery of the Muslim soldiers in the HVO and their linking up with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Armija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the witness has understood that this relates to paragraph 7. Right. Go on, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was exactly the point that I was going to make. I thought the witness was quite, quite clear in indicating his interpretation of paragraph 7, and went on to say something to the effect, "I could quite understand in those circumstances." So it seemed to me there was a fair contextual reading of the document. If we could then go on, please, to P 04756.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'll let you find the document. I do have one further questions for you about the previous topic; although, they're actually related to the next document as well. Again, trying to tie together now some of the concepts and principles that we've talked about for the last two days, once General Petkovic issued the order, 3019, that we were just talking about, I mean, is that the end of his responsibility; or as a senior commander, once you've given that order, what is further incumbent upon you to do?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order could only be seen as a -- I mean, as far as rounding up the Muslims are concerned, it's -- it's almost what we would describe as a warning order or an initial order, because it carries no detail at all of how it's to be done and how it's to be supported. So if, for whatever reason, the order goes out like this, then I would expect the Main Staff to be working frantically to follow up that with supplementary orders, is what we call them, supplementary orders, amplifying the detail of how this should be conducted, what the logistic arrangements would be, where the camps are going to be, who is going to provide food, water, et cetera et, cetera et, cetera. So this is not the end. This is just the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, having gone on then to Exhibit 4 -- P 04756.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This -- these are the minutes of a defence department meeting held on the 2nd of September, 1993. And for present purposes, well, let's stay on the topic of the operation of detention facilities. If I can direct your attention to page 4, about halfway down the page in English under -- it's item number 3. And, then, going about halfway down the page it makes reference -- well, just so we can see who is talking, it's talking about Coric and the head, Stojic, and then Coric it says: "Coric then put forward some of the problem encountered by the military police." And in that context, skipping several lines, it then says: "Military prisons are another example of very bad work. The head, then the document is referring to Mr. Stojic, "the head took the floor and then said, 'My opinion is that we have two military prisoners, Heliodrom and the military prison at Ljubuski. As the other places where detainees are held, Gabela and Dretelj, I do not consider them as military facilities and refuse to personally endorse the work of these institutions.'" Now, my question to you on that point, General, is tying this back into, again, Exhibit P 03019. That order, having been given, 3019, can you comment on the statement attributed to Mr. Stojic, which says essentially, "I don't take on any responsibility for at least these other facilities, Gabela and Dretelj"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there appears to me to be a mismatch here, because the initiating order, if I can put it like that, signed by chief of the HVO Main Staff, Major General Petkovic, initiating the rounding up of these people into places unspecified in that order was a military order issued to military units. It would be, therefore, my assumption that those military units carried out those orders and are now in charge of the detainees. I don't know, but that's what the assumption from that very brief order would be. And, therefore, all the -- these people that are being detained are -- whether they're in a military prison, are not are the responsibility of the military and, indeed, are the responsibility of the initiating officer Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we can then move further, just actually a couple of days later, this document is dated concerning a meeting on the 2nd of September [Realtime transcript read in error "December"], 1993. And if we could move to another set of minutes, Exhibit P 04841, for the 6th of September [Realtime transcript read in error "December"], 1993, four days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my colleague Mr. Scott, but I think there's an error in the transcript. It says "December" in the transcript instead of "September," so perhaps that should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right. It is, indeed, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. I don't know if I misspoke or if it was a matter of translation or transcription. In any event, counsel is correct. The dates were in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that in mind, General, if you have -- if you've been able to find that document, P 04841, you will see on the -- excuse me. Bottom of page 1, there's an agenda given, then there's something that's been written here as AD1. I don't know if that's Article 1. But, in any event, it says: "On the basis of verbal reports and insights gained into the manner of executing punishments and conditions of detention of persons capture as active-duty and reserve enemy forces and persons preparing an armed rebellion, the situation was declared unsatisfactory..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "...the situation was declared unsatisfactory and harmful to the reputation and interest of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. "It was also concluded that the responsibility for the present situation does not lie with the HVO of the HZ HB (government of the HR HB). However, in order to avoid the situation being used in ways that are adverse to the political and other interests of Herceg-Bosna, valid principles of international law of war and international humanitarian law need to be observed in executing punishments and implementing other measures." These were in a meeting as indicated here with Mr. Prlic presiding and signing the minutes as -- on the last day -- on the last page as president of the government. I just want to put the question to you, similar to the question about the minutes of the earlier meeting involving Mr. Coric and Mr. Stojic. I note that in this same meeting, if we look at the first page, those in attendance, if the record is correct, Mr. Stojic was also at this meeting. When it makes a statement that was concluded that "the responsibility does not rest with us," can you comment, again, on the -- where -- what responsibility did the HVO, having gone down this road, take on? For holding and caring for these prisoners and detainees, persons that were being held, what responsibilities had been undertaken at that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Just one second. Now, when he's talking about the HVO. What exactly is he talking about? The military or is he talking about civilian government? The gentleman, there is to foundation thus far, that he has explored and understood and is able and is capable to discuss how the civilian government was structured. Now he's being asked to look at a particular document, and from there to drive certain conclusions based on his military expertise. I dare say there has been no foundation laid. Also, in the very last paragraph of this document, it clearly shows: "Since Mr. Boban the Supreme Commander of the HR HB armed forces has not been consulted on the matter, it was decided that he should be." Now, obviously, there are all sorts of events going on. I have no objections to the gentleman giving opinions based on military matters. But when he's asked to give an opinion as to a document such as this, without having, at least in my opinion, having laid a foundation that he is capable of rendering a decision, based on knowledge of how the civilian government functioned vis-a-vis the military, I think that is beyond the scope of the witness's ability to answer and, therefore, I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can address, Your Honour, perhaps with some additional foundational questions. I hope not to take too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But in the reports - and, of course, as I said yesterday, we haven't had the time to go through every part of your report in detail - but in terms of your curriculum vitae, which we discussed yesterday, is it correct, sir, that a substantial amount of both the training that you have received and the training you have given to others has involved, I think it was put at one point, dealing with the senior military political interface?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what is your -- what is the general experience or information you can provide to us in terms of how in this instance, for example, let's start with 2, the military head, and that is in this instance either Mr. -- because we're now talking about a period that spans from the end of June to September of 1993, first Mr. Petkovic and then Mr. Praljak as the military held, the top military officer, how that person then relates to the top civilian defence official, the head of the defence department, Mr. Stojic? Let's start with that in your experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, if I may, and I don't mean to be disruptive of the proceedings, but, again, a foundation needs to be laid because there's a transitional period. You have the Croatian Community, then you have the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Clearly, the gentleman is capable of discussing how it is, how things are in the UK or perhaps in other Western European countries or NATO government, because he has had some experience, but we're dealing with a unique situation. What I'm saying here is: Before he gets to answer those sorts of questions, at least a foundation needs to be laid as to what documents he's reviewed. What is his basic knowledge with respect to this particular government, the way it's set up, this system. And then from there, if we're satisfied, I have no objections. But I think that we're getting a lit bit ahead of ourselves to simply say: Since he's been trained on how civilian governments interact with the military, therefore, in this instance, this is the way it operated. First, he must demonstrate that he has knowledge of how this particular political system, such as it was, at least de jure existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, there is a document that we all have before us. I presume what you want to ask the military expert is something of a military nature, and that is why you're presenting that document. What is the actual question that you wish to raise? Because here we're talking about the government meeting under the Presidency of Mr. Prlic at Mostar on the 6th of September, 10.00 a.m., and the meeting ends at 12.00 noon. So this is a government meeting. What is the military question that you wish to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just referring in sort, so that I can deal with the foundational questions, perhaps at least very, very briefly. The Chamber may refer to, in the general's report, for example - and I will not have found all of them in the last two minutes as I have you've stood here on my feet - but, for example, at paragraph number 10. About halfway through paragraph number 10, he talks about the course content was set at the strategic -- strategic level. This is at the Royal College of Defence Studies. The course content was set at the strategic level and involved considerable study around the politico-military interface. Then, beyond that, I think there's a number of other places where he talks about that. In paragraph 14, he also -- at the end of paragraph 14, he also talks about the military-political interface. Then, when we get further into his report, in effect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Statements having been made, just very, very briefly. In paragraph 25, he talks about the decree on armed forces and says, in effect, this enshrines political control over the military as one would expect. And, in paragraph 26, he talks about the consultation. The overall military commander would be expected to interact directly or indirectly with the political commander-in-chief. Then, he talks about: "In the HZ HB, it is my opinion that the overall commander would interact with the head of the defence department on a regular basis and with the president as Supreme Commander." So just so it's clear, in the report, the expert has addressed these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The point in showing the current exhibit, P 04841, is to ask, first of all: Would it surprise you, sir, at the most senior levels at the military-political level that a serious problem would be discussed not only by -- on the military side, but that would carry over onto the political leadership as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I maintain my objection. I'll just -- I'll let it stand. I have a moving objection, a continuing objection to this line of questioning. A foundation has not been laid. He's being asked -- I have no objections with the gentleman having a background on the interface. I'm sure he's had to deal with, you know, the Defence Minister in the UK, whatever the situation may be, but that's not the point. The point is: We're dealing with a particular political structure on the ground. Has he looked at the way it functions? Has he looked at these documents? Is he capable of giving an opinion? Because he's being asked these very specific questions. I have a continuing objection to the competency of this witness to provide these sorts of answers, and I will sit down for the sake of going forward; otherwise, I would be objecting to every question of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what I don't really perceive is what is it exactly you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just ask the question, because that will make things clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you Mr. President. In reference to the language that I read out of these minutes some time ago, and I'm not presenting as hypothetical, I'm reading a document, I'm reading an HVO record. In attendance, among others, are Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, and others as listed on the minutes, and I've read the part of the record on the second page of the English version, starting really at the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I guess, really, after all this discussion, my question to the general is: General, does it surprise you that at -- if there is a sufficiently serious level that would come up on the military side, that ultimately would find its way, as it does here on the 6th of September, 1993, being discussed at a level of government that involves both the president of the government and the defence minister and others -- or the Head of the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't surprise me that it's being discussed at all. We seem to have the situation in accordance with the previous document, where a military order has been given to military units, to round up large numbers of Muslim people. I don't think anyone has questioned that. What we have questioned is whether there was sufficient logistic support for that operation. It would appear from this document that there is now, as a result of that happening, severe concern that things had are going wrong, and the international laws of war and humanitarian law are not being complied with. What strikes me as surprising is that military order, having been given and carried out, and Mr. Boban being the Supreme Commander of the HR HB armed forces as well, is that this meeting concludes that really this has nothing to do with us, seen in light of the military is subservient to the political.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we can then continue on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just have a clarification on this point. Do you read this passage, the second paragraph on page 2 in the English version, as saying that the political authority, the government, says it's none of our business, implying that it is the exclusive responsibility of the military? Is that your interpretation of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's how I am reading this: Responsibility of the present situation does not lie with the HVO Croatian Defence council of the HZ HB government. That is what I'm taking that to mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to follow on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to follow on and finish this particular set of documents, if you could then go on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. I'm a little bit troubled by the answer that was just given. General, we are talking about the document 4841. That is a conclusion from which -- that is the document from which you derive your conclusion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this document, as we see it before our very eyes, relates to a government meeting that was held under the presidency of Mr. Prlic, who was the president. There is an agenda for that meeting. It is set out here; and, in item 1, they're going to deal with the question of the situation arising from the measures to be taken to isolate persons, prisoners of war, to implement International Law on War. And then item 2, miscellaneous. Then we see that item 1 is based on verbal reports and that there are going to be decisions taken by the government or -- or in point 1, in the conclusions, the place for the detention of prisoners of war must be determined, and the Ministry for Defence is going to be in charge of that, and it has 15 days to do so. But people must be punished. Here, again, the Ministry for Defence and for Justice and the administration are responsible, and they have 15 days, and the Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees, et cetera, is also. Here, we come back to logistics: Take measures concerning quantities of food, sanitation, et cetera. And on -- in point 2, under miscellaneous, there are other secondary topics relating to students and so on and so forth. So where do you see that nothing has been decided? That's what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was simply referring to the second paragraph on page 2, where it said: "It was also concluded that the responsibility for the present situation does not lie with the HVO Croatian Defence Council." I said I found that quite surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should be noted, however, that we find it quite surprising that the gentleman hasn't read any of the documents concerning how the government was structured, then that might cause a surprise that he has right now. That's part of the problem. When he's talking about government, what is he talking about? What is his understanding of the council vis-a-vis Mr. Boban and the Presidency? What is the distinction? There lies the problem. So he's looking at it from the UK mind frame. He's looking at it from the traditional approach that he understands how government functions in the UK, not in the way the government was functioning back then. I go back to my earlier discussion. I have no objections to the gentleman opining on this, but we need to lay a foundation. He's simply not competent. He lacks the knowledge, and he lacks the knowledge because he wasn't provided with the necessary information by the Prosecution, if he was going to go into this area. I also raise an objection, and the objection is this, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... he prepared a report. Now he's being shown documents that were outside of what he was shown in preparation of the report. We're entitled to notice as -- if he's going to be going into documents and opinions as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To end, General, and then I'll give the floor to Mr. Scott, when you say reading paragraph 2 of page 2, that it is up to the HVO, is there a political connotation here? Doesn't that mean that it's responsibility for the events that occurred, and that has nothing to do with themselves taking on their own responsibilities? Because later on they do take decisions. If they were not responsible, why would they later on take decisions? Aren't you interpreting things somewhat in paragraph 2? Although, I do, of course, understand given the little time you've had, that you've come to those conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm simply saying, Your Honour, that the original order for rounding up all these people was a military order. It would be reasonable, I believe, to expect that order to have been given, not as an isolated military action but as a politico-military action. And in the light of that, the fact that the HVO Croatian Defence Council now declares that it doesn't seem to have got any response for what's happened so far, even though, using its own words, "there are transgressions of international law plainly taking place," I find surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do -- I do apologise for rising, but a point does come where the level of assumptions must be explained. It can't simply be stated and taken as anything approaching anything that you -- Your Honours can rely upon without a foundation or without something further being explained. I do note, of course, and it is a matter that I won't belabour now, that there does appear to have been movement in relation to the witness, because Judge Trechsel's comments, with respect, was very clear. The witness spoke in relation to that. He answered that, and he says later on, in relation to Mr. President's question, that he found that state surprising. That does appear to be an evolution in his account. But, Your Honour, the assumptions that the detention came from the political side of -- of control needs to be explained. It hasn't been. It's simply an assumption, and it's there that I think Mr. Karnavas does have point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott, if I take this a bit further, but perhaps there is a possibility to reconcile the views. On the one hand, we have the sentence that astonishes the witness. And if you look at what it talks about, it is the present situation. It is looking backwards. Then, with the conclusion, the government is looking forward and is devising measures. I find that to -- to be clearly visible in the document itself, and I do not see that it is in any way speculative to read it as it is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, all these, of course, are matters for closing speeches and for arguments, but what is objected to is without -- Your Honours need to be assisted by having an expert opinion from an extremely able army officer that has proper foundations that Your Honours are clear about. Now, the evidence so far is that Bruno Stojic has said that only two prison camps are part of his responsibility, or that there are two prison camps. Then he also states in this political meeting that they abhor violations taking place. Then we seek to jump into a million miles and say, Well, the order of detention is a political decision. It seems to fly in the face of the facts on the documents before you. Now, if the witness then seeks to speculate, the basis of that speculation must be based upon an understanding of the context that Your Honours are deliberating upon, rather than just an abstract understanding of what happens in a regular organised army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps you could help me out. I do not see any, any sentences here attributed to Mr. Stojic, except for the passage regarding students. Maybe I missed something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the inference from the Prosecution - and this is why I understand that my learned friend Mr. Scott emphasised that Mr. Stojic was present at this meeting - it's seeking to impute the actions in the field and the detention that took place to the political side of the community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, that needs to be explained, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, counsel. You have just said that here Mr. Stojic said this or that about the problem we are interested in. We're not interested in a student. I'm asking you where does it say here that Mr. Stojic said this or that? I think you're making an assumption here. Where is it here in this , in this report on the meeting, except for page 3 at the bottom, where is it said that something has been stated by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, lead counsel very helpfully provides P 04756.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We're dealing with 4841. That's the document we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was very clear, in my respectful submission, from the evidence elicited by the Prosecution at page 59, line 17 -- bear with me. I think it's line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of the LiveNote transcript, and this was the reference between Bruno Stojic, that there were only two prisons, Gabela and Dretelj, that were considered as military facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That was not -- that was of not this meeting, Counsel. I am sorry. I think we should go on now let Mr. Scott continue his cross-examination, because we're --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you must give me a chance, because what my learned friend, Mr. Scott, quite clearly was seeking to do was to compare -- it was a specific question. He was seeking to compare the political meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not reading his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me go to Mr. Scott's question. It's very clear, because he was cross-referencing that suggestion by Bruno Stojic with his presence in the meeting, and seeking to obtain conclusions in relation to that. Your Honour, that's all I've got to say. The question can be put. I've put my remarks forward, but it goes down to the lack of foundation in relation to attributing the detention that took place to the political events that took place in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It is as simple as that, and it goes down to my learned friend Mr. Karnavas's question regarding proper foundation. Your honour, I can't take it further. I think it is very straightforward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to make a correction. I tried to tell my colleague Ms. Nozica, but I didn't succeed. I think that Mr. Kahn made a slight mistake, because Bruno Stojic in the document we mentioned acknowledged as authority over prison Heliodrom and Ljubuski, and not Gabela and Dretelj, as was recorded in the transcript on page 73, line 15 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just before putting the next question to the witness. Just to be ever-so brief in my time in comparison to the Defence time on these points will be ever-so short. The reason that the -- the connection between -- there were all sorts of objections and issues being raised about the connection between the political and the military. The reason was -- part of the reason showing these documents to the witness and asking these questions, in an abbreviated way, because one of the problems, of course, is we can't present the entire case through this witness, and all the other documents and all the other meetings which took place between the end of June and September. We can't do that. We'd be here for days. Now, ultimately, maybe we'll all have an opportunity to go through day by day all: The international demands that were being made, the testimony by Ambassador Galbraith raising demarches about the conditions in this, before this meeting took place. There's all sorts of evidence we don't have time to consider today. The only point here is to say, in this particular respect, in this particular chain of documents, and it's not I don't think it surprises anyone, you have the link between the top military commander, at this time being either Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic being the person who gave the order we looked at earlier, and the head of the -- the political head, the civilian head of the defence department, in one meeting; and then going to another top government meeting, the meeting of the HVO government, at which Mr. Stojic then goes from the earlier meeting with his commanders, with the people in the chain of command, Coric and others, then goes to another meeting at the top of the government in which also Mr. Prlic and other ministers are other heads are involved. I don't think that should surprise anyone, and that was the reason for bringing Mr. Stojic in. I don't think that there's any interpretation of the structures of government or anything. That's what the record is -- it's what these documents say, and that's the only point that we were just saying it, up to the point of then what the President's already covered and Judge Trechsel, and that is that the witness's reaction to looking at those particular minutes. I think we have answered it now and we can go forward, but I just wanted to make it clear that I just think some of the objections are not well-founded, Your Honour. Now, if we could go on to finish up on this particular set of documents to Exhibit P 05104. In fairness to everyone, at the end of that meeting there was reference to the fact, well, Mr. Boban isn't here, so we should consult with Mr. Boban. Well, this is the Prosecution trying to be fair and trying to continue the story. A few days later on the 15th of September, about nine days later, Mr. Boban apparently issues an order, calling for all the HVO military and armed forces to make sure that they're complying with all the stands of international law, et cetera et cetera. Item 3, General, if you have that - I'm sorry, in my haste I've gone quite quickly - but if you now turn to Exhibit 5104. If I can direct your attention to the second page of the English version, paragraph 3: "In the prisoners of war detention centres, where the conditions required by the International War of Law," presumably, "and the Geneva Conventions are not ensured, they should immediately be introduced, and prisoners of war must be treated in accordance with provisions of the Geneva Convention and other humanitarian standards." Now, is there anything surprising to you, General, about the fact that it would be recognised or further recognised that the Geneva Conventions and the Laws of War would apply to the holding of either prisoners of war or other detained persons?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression on this is full marks to Mr. Boban for taking a grip of the situation and ensuring that the correct conditions are applied in accordance with the laws required.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in further, on this issue that we've gotten into in the last hour, perhaps, on the political-military interface, can I ask you to look at item 7 of Mr. Boban's order: "The HVO Main Staff will inform all subordinated commands and units of this had order and provide professional help in its implementation." Is that the sort of -- my question to you, having read that, is: Is that the sort of military-political interface that you might expect in this situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the chain of command that we referred to earlier on this morning, starting with the president. Here we have Boban, as the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, issuing orders down through the HVO Main Staff for implementation down to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In point 7, it says that that should be implemented, but what? What is to be implemented in its implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I think it says "this order," Your Honour. Your Honour, I see it's 12.30, and what might be the most efficient way is now what I would like to be able to do is to focus exactly on the final documents I'd like to put to the witness, if I could do that during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, do you want to break now or do you want to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it might be most helpful and efficient, Your Honour, if we took the breakdown, so I could then identify the final several exhibits to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. You will have 30 minutes left, because you've already used up three hours, 30 minutes, and a few more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I think that we've abbreviated the final Prosecution questions, and I think we can finish in the next few minutes. Before I do that, if I can just deal a couple of outstanding matters that the Chamber has raised. In connection with, Your Honour Mr. President, your point this morning about Exhibit 301, we have indeed confirmed that Exhibit P 00425 is a much better and complete version of that same document. We can certainly -- we can either tender both or we can tender P 00425 in place of P 00301, whichever suits the Chamber. But there is, indeed, a much better and full copy of that, number one. That's just been -- that has been provided to the Chamber, I think, handed out a few moments ago and should be -- and also to the Defence. Secondly, Judge Trechsel yesterday, I believe, if I have this correct - I may be mistaken, but we also try to be responsive to the Judges' questions and inquiries - in connection with Exhibit P 00307, it's the one in which unfortunately we only had limited translation, we did find in that same document, which the Prosecution does indeed tender in its entirety, an explicit reference in chapter 2, Article 26, chapter 2, Article 26, on page 9 of the Croatian or B/C/S version, and it may correspond to something that Judge Trechsel raised yesterday. It's a matter of reading the document. I'm sure I will be correct if I misrepresent the document, but that reference appears to state: "A military is not obliged to carry out orders directed against the constitutional order of the HR HB and is not obliged to carry out other actions that are unlawful and have characteristics of a criminal offence."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe, if I put that in the form of a question to the

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: point I showed you a document, and you said something to the effect that that more or less reflected or enshrined the general principle in modern armies, that a subordinate is required to carry out the orders of a superior except for an illegal order.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In fact, he has a duty not to carry out an illegal order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the reference to chapter 2, Article 26 of Exhibit P 00307 that I've just read out would be consistent with that; is that correct? You won't have it in translation, I'm afraid, sir. We haven't had a chance to --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you read it out, that's consistent with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finishing on two just -- very quickly on two exhibits. They both relate to topics that have been raised in the last two days, if I can ask you to look, please, at P 05134. My question, General, is really quite limited. But in light of the conversation we've had today about the Main Staff of control of certain assets, this is a report from a duty operations officer, dated the 16th of September, 1993. And on the first page, on the first two items, if I can just direct your attention to a decision on operations: "An H203 shelled Jugobanka, self-propelled cannon fired on Pucine, and a hand-held rocket launcher fired on the theatre, a T-130 fired on Gornje Selo and Nazdrijica Mahala, as authorised by the chief of artillery of the Main Staff." The next item: "An H122, a Garista, fired on a convoy of lorries entering Blagaj as authorised by the Main Staff." So can I just simply ask you: Would that be consistent with your earlier statements to the Chamber about the Main Staff control of heavier weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be consistent with the Main Staff having control of these sorts of weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to go to Exhibit P 07044.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, on this one, I'm afraid, with apologies again, that we have -- the date has been mistranslated. It should say, if you want to correct it, it should say 6 December 1992. I'm sorry I've been corrected, too. I apologise, Your Honour. Apparently, It's not the first time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In any event, the point being -- the only really point of this being, General, if you can look at that exhibit, 7044, again, this is a document issued over the name of Milivoj Petkovic: "Order: Number 1, send regular daily combat reports twice a day as follows: A morning report by 0800 hours," in other words 8.00 a.m., "and an evening report by 2200 hours," or 10.00 p.m., following the list of directives in attachment one." We can look at it, if anyone wants it, it's the guidelines for -- in fact, if we look at the attachment 1, several pages down in the English version, it says: "Guidelines for daily combat report with list of questions." In just looking at this General, and not just those parts but if you scan through the rest of the document, would that put -- be putting into place a form of command reporting, coming up the chain of command that would -- you would find nothing unusual about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing unusual. That's exactly what you would expect to see. That's how the higher headquarters gets a good handle on what is going on and what needs to be done, what logistic resupply needs to be done. That's how the higher headquarters controls the support required for subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Then, in terms of the distribution, we have it going out to essentially all military districts and then some of the more specialised units that we've talked about earlier today; for example, Bruno Busic, Ludvig Pavlovic, the Artillery Rocket Regiment, et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, in conclusion, I'm going to direct you to paragraph 79 and 80 of your report and ask you: In recognising as you do the -- some of the challenges and difficulties facing the HVO in the situation that existed at the time, you conclude at the end of paragraph 79: "A working governmental system, with a military answerable to the civilian leadership and with orders and instructions flowing down the chain of command from the Presidency via the department of defence and the Main Staff to the operational commands," essentially in your opinion, that existed at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents that I have referenced and read, that is my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And since you wrote the report in March and you signed it, I believe, in March of 2006, you continue to stand by those conclusions, again, based on the documents and information available to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 80, you -- you likewise then conclude: "A working army subject to laid down military code of discipline was plainly in existence." Skipping a couple of lines. "That said, there are doctrinal documents, particularly those pertaining to compliance with the international laws of war, that had they been followed would have resulted in reasonable military behaviour. The onus on commanders to set a proper example and insist on proper standards of discipline was great." Do you continue to stand by that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General Pringle, on behalf of the Prosecution, I want to thank you for coming to The Hague and providing your evidence to the Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence for cross-examination, I'd like to draw your attention to Document 8128, Mr. Scott. It's a document we were shown yesterday; and, overnight, I realised that the annex -- the documents annexed to this exhibit, organisational charts, that they had not been translated into English. In other words, I do not have the translation in English of the documents that are to be found in the B/C/S version of the document, and these documents relate, among other things, to the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need these documents. You requested the admission of Exhibit 8128, and I'd like to know what is written in these boxes in these charts --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or in these squares or rectangles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can assure the Chamber -- I assure the Chamber that you will have a full translation as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now for the Defence, who will start? Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to say good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom, and I'd like to ask the usher's assistance. Could he please distribute the documents that I'm going to use in the cross-examination. The first three copies are for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Pringle.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My name is Senka Nozica, and together with Mr. Karim Khan, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Bruno Stojic. That is my binder of documents, and I'll move on to the documents very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before we begin, I'd like to say that I have 30 minutes for my cross-examination, and I have been given another 15 minutes from Mr. Karnavas from Mr. Prlic's Defence team. I hope that will suffice and will take us to the end of business today. If not, then we'll go on tomorrow morning. But I say this because I know Mr. Karnavas asked for a little time to be left over for him to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, when it comes to the internal set-up and organisation of the defence department, the Prosecution showed you two documents as far as I was able to note, and could you look for it, please. It is document P 0729, and it is the third document from the bottom, from the end, P 0729. Just let me know what you've found it, please, P 0729.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got P 0729. I assume there's an English translation at the back, is there? Yes. Okay. Got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Now, in attachment A, to your findings, are documents are mentioned that you received from the Prosecution in order to write your report; and on that list, that list includes this document and the date when it was filed is mentioned. It is the 20th of May, 1993. Now, in the original, in the Croatian version of the document, as we can see, you don't have page 1. You don't have the first name -- first page, but translation is complete. At the end of the original document in Croatian, and we can see this on e-court as well, on our screens, the date is the 10th of November, 1992. There's a number there, which is 666/92. And in the translation of the document, on number 1, the date is stated as the 20th of May, 1993; whereas, on the last page the date is the 1st of June, 1993, and the reference number is 007/93. Now, Mr. Pringle, quite obviously, you were given the wrong translation of the document. That's something we noticed, and we informed the Prosecution thereof. In fact, what you received was the translation of another document, a different document, which you did have an opportunity to see. It is, in fact, a document dated the 20th of May, 1993, and the number is P 02477. Now, I'd like to ask you to take a look at the translation of the document which you were supplied the wrong translation of, and we translated the document. I'm sure that the Prosecution will also have its own translation in due course. But for the purposes of our cross-examination we translated the document, so it is 2D 00567. That's the number of that document, and you will find it in my binder. It is the last document. So would you have a look at that translation, which is the last document. You have the Croatian version first, and following that you have the translation in English. Have you found that document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the English translation here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a decision on the internal organisation of the defence department, as it says. The date is the 17th of October, 1992, and I'd like to draw your attention to just a few important points in that decision. To begin with, the preamble, where it says that the decision follows a provision or article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. But as you started off with the dates, I cannot help noticing that in the end here, where Mate Boban signed, the date is 10th of November. Now, you're certainly able to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have very little time, and I consider this to be a very important matter. There are quite a number of things that might not be clear, but I'll explain them in due course when I get to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the preamble, it says that this decision is based on Article 14 of the decision of the president of the HZ HB on the basic principles of organisation of the defence department, number 599/92, of October the 15th, 1992. Now, my question is this: Were you shown this basic decision, upon which this decision on internal organisation was founded? So were you shown the decision of the 15th of September, counsel said, 1992? Yes, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. If that's one of the references in my report, the answer would be yes. If it's not, the answer may be yes or no. But straight off the top of my head, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'll show you the decision in due course, and then you can tell me whether you remember having seen it or not. Now, to move on, this decision, in paragraph I, regulates the internal organisation of sectors, administrations, office, and the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council's defence department. Another thing I'd like to mention regarding this decision is that the decision was brought by the -- the head of the defence department, Bruno Stojic, in agreement with the president of the HZ HB, Mate Boban. He approved it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, that is the only logical explanation that this reference number of Mr. Boban and the date, the date that he signed this decision, that that's it, and when he gave his approval. I consider that to be logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As I said, this relates to internal organisation in 1992. That is the 1992 decision. And in the attachment to your report, you were able to see the following decision, which comes after this one, and that is the decision which was numbered P 02477, which in my binder is marked with a yellow sticker. It's the third yellow sticker. Sir, you can just take a look and see if you have already seen this decision and can comment. I'd just like to remind you that it is the decision whose translation -- the translation of which you saw, but it was wrongly attached to P 00729. Do you remember having seen that decision before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, not specifically, but I would keep referring you back to my report and to see whether it's one of the reference documents. You remember that I wrote that report in March 2006, I think it was. So you're showing me a document from cold and you're asking me if I've ever seen it before. That's quite difficult. If it's referenced in my report, then I would have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, it's very important for me to ask you that for the following reason: In your findings, you comment on certain relationships between the Supreme Commander, the Main Staff, and the defence department. So all I want to do is to establish which documents you used which helped you to provide your opinions, and the document, as I say, is in one of your references --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, wait a moment. Document P 0729, are you sure it exists? Because if we look into the e-court system, this document does not appear to exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P 02477 is the document number, Your Honour. P 02477.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: P 024467, you've got it numbered as.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Would you look at the end of that document? We have the document on e-court; and at the end of that document, it says that the document of the 17th of October is placed adacta, and Bruno Stojic took the decision, and Mr. Mate Boban agreed that it shall no longer be effective. Now, let's look at another document which was the basis for the enactment of these two other documents. Let's look at it together. It is P 00586, and it is the second document from the beginning of my binder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Nozica. If you planned to leave these documents, it would be helpful to point out the difference between one and the other, because there is one number more in one of them, in this -- this one we had last, which has 15 and the other has 14 numbers. Which is one that is additional? Because if it's -- there must be something relevant to it in order to give the difference between the documents a meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these documents speak about the internal organisation of the defence department. One is dated October 1992, and one is dated May 1993. Now, there was certain changes with respect to organisation, and so some additions were made, new sectors, new offices, and so on. But I did not consider that that was essential for this cross-examination. I didn't feel it necessary to point out the changes and amendments. All I want to learn from the witness is which documents he was presented with, in order to see how the defence department was organised. So for the purposes of this cross-examination, I didn't point out the differences. They will come into play later on when I shall point them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'll be interested to see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found the document P 00586, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Now, I'm going to ask you to look at the title page and the first page. It says the 17th of October, 1992, does it not, but this is the attending document. I'd now like to move on to the actual first page, where we see that this is a decision on the internal organisation of the defence department, and we've already seen this in court. It has the status of an exhibit. Let's look at the date on the last page when this document was passed -- compiled and passed; and as we see, it is the 15th of September, 1992. But this decision was taken by the president of the HZ HB, Mate Boban, so it is a decision on the basic principles of organisation of the defence department, as it says. I'll give you some time to look through it if you need it, because I think it is a fundamental document which relates to the organisation of the department and the relationships of the Supreme Command of the department and the head and the Main Staff. What I want to know how is, first: Have you seen this document before? Was it shown you when you were asked to find your findings and report, and does it remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just say that if you're going to continuously ask me from cold if I've seen a document before because you're referring to something in the report I've written, maybe you could refer me to my report and I will see whether it's footnoted, and then I will be able to give you a sensible answer on that. Just being shown a document and being asked have I ever seen it before, I can't give you a sensible answer to that. So you probably know whether I've been shown it before because you would have read my report and you will have know seen it was footnoted or not. So if we work from my report, I'll be able to give you a sensible answer on whether I've seen it before. That said, would you like know now to read this document? Is there any specific part you want to draw my attention to?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From your report, it appears that you have not seen this document before. Let me make that clear straight away, that from your findings it does not follow that you've seen this document before. I would like to drawn your attention to two facts. First of all, it is a document of the president of the HZ HB, that it was passed in September, that you were shown the document on the basic principles of internal organisation of the defence department, which was passed on the basis of this particular document. So now take a look at paragraph 9 of the document, which relates to relationships between the Main Staff, the Supreme Commander, and the defence department or the head of the defence department, and then I'll tie that up with certain things you say in your report, so that we can see whether the descriptions given in the document are, in fact, the relationships that you describe in your findings. So that is the reason that I'm showing you this document.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please, would you please speak close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The wrong microphone was switched on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, I'm just interested in paragraph 9 or point 9; and once you've read through it, I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a document regulating these relationships; that is to say, relationships between the Supreme Commander, the head of the defence department -- and the head of the defence department of the Main Staff. Now, you dealt with that in paragraphs 25, 26, and 79 of your report. You addressed that issue. Would you like to refresh your memory? If so, those are the paragraphs, 26, 25 -- or rather, 25, 26. I'm referring to the last portions of paragraph 25 and 26, where you refer to the president of to the defence department and the political leadership up to the Main Staff. In paragraph 79, this was something that the Prosecutor asked you just a little while ago, you say towards the end that the orders and instructions were passed down the chain of command from the Presidency to the defence department, the Main Staff, and the operational commands. Now, my question to you is as follows: The relationship you described there, is it in keeping with the prescribed relationship as set out in the document you've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
